claims.text: Removing one or more constituents from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alters short-range chemical order.
Removing one or more constituents from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alters local lattice distortions.
Changes in local chemical order can alter the spatial distribution of stacking-fault energies.
Local lattice distortions influence stacking-fault-energy distributions.
Local chemical order can modify dislocation behavior and lattice resistance to dislocation motion.
Stacking-fault energy controls whether FCC alloys deform through perfect-dislocation slip, mechanical twinning, or strain-induced martensitic transformation.
The equiatomic quinary alloy has an intermediate stacking-fault energy of approximately 25–30 mJ/m² and deforms by both dislocation slip and mechanical twinning.
Activation of mechanical twinning can increase strain hardening and thereby improve strength and ductility.
Element removal from the quinary alloy changes dislocation-core configurations.
Composition-induced changes in stacking-fault energy and dislocation behavior cause differences in work hardening among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Composition-induced changes in stacking-fault energy and dislocation behavior cause differences in yield strength among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Composition-induced changes in stacking-fault energy and dislocation behavior cause differences in ductility among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.

The controlled comparison will use equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys processed to remain single-phase FCC, with processing history, grain size, test temperature, and strain rate matched.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit different work-hardening responses.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit shifts in yield strength.
Relative to the quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit variations in ductility.
Mechanical-property differences across the alloys will correlate with changes in stacking-fault energies and dislocation configurations observed during deformation.
The magnitude and direction of property changes may depend on which particular elements are removed.
The hypothesis is restricted to room-temperature, matched-strain-rate comparisons of controlled-grain-size, single-phase FCC materials produced through matched thermomechanical processing.

If the alloys retain different mechanical properties but show no statistically significant differences in lattice distortion, stacking-fault-energy distributions, or dislocation behavior, the proposed mediator mechanism is falsified.
